newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai baht shaky, but still attractive - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht shaky, but still attractive - analysts.

text.p: Thailand's baht, hit by rounds of heavy speculative selling, still is an attractive alternative to other Asian currencies, analysts said on Monday.

Despite Thailand's current political uncertainty and economic woes, which have made the baht shaky and vulnerable, its relative stability against the dollar and peg to high interest rates make it attractive, they said.
"The outlook for the baht is not good right now due to underlying economic and political problems," said Bank of Asia vice president Montira Utarapichat.

"But the interest rate gap between the dollar and baht of about 500 basis points and the central bank's strict control on the dollar/baht exchange rate are to the baht's advantage over the (Indonesian) rupiah and (Malaysian) ringgit," she said.
The Bank of Thailand fixes the daily foreign exchange rate based on a basket of major currencies. It traded at 25.34-35 to the U.S. dollar late on Monday.

The baht has been under selling pressure over the past few months due to concerns among foreign investors over the sagging economy, slow export growth, a widening currenct account deficit and political uncertainty.

"Offshore speculators usually attack currencies of countries which are facing serious economic problems. Thailand's recent economic and financial chaos put the baht on their list of regional currencies to speculate against," said a senior dealer at a local bank.

The chronic economic problems triggered market speculation that the government may devalue the baht in an effort to boost the economy and lift exports. The finance ministry and the Bank of Thailand denied the devaluation rumours.
The baht's gloom was exacerberated last Tuesday after Moody's Investors Service downgraded Thailand's short-term sovereign debt ratings.

But the analysts said the recent speculative attack on the baht appeared to be marked by caution following the Bank of Thailand's promise to defend the currency from any possible attack in the future.

"The central bank's serious intention to defend the baht and Thailand's large foreign reserve of about $40 billion will make offshore players think twice about speculating against the currency," said one economist at a local bank.
Early last month, the central bank took an unprecedented step to calm the nervous foreign exchange and money markets by intervening to prop up the currency.
Again last Friday, the central bank injected several billion baht into the money market to stabilise the currency when it was under pressure from devaluation talk again.
Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond later vowed to make any possible intervention in spot and forward currency swap markets to protect the baht from any future attack.
The governor said defending the baht wass one of the basic missions of the central bank, and an attack on the baht would be considered a direct attack on the BOT itself.
